The Black-Powder Wars, 1618–1877

Nine battles from Gustavus Adolphus at Lützen in 1632 to the Wagon Box Fight in 1867: the Thirty Years' War, the American Revolution, the Peninsula and the War of 1812, the storming of the Great Redan before Sevastopol, the first battle of the American Civil War, and two fights on the Bozeman Trail against the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the armies' figures for five eras, the wound tables their battles roll on, and the battlefields.

The battlefields: Lützen 1632, Cowpens 1781, Albuera 1811, Lundy's Lane 1814, The Great Redan, 18 June 1855, The Great Redan, 8 September 1855, First Bull Run 1861, The Fetterman Fight 1866, The Wagon Box Fight 1867.

What is switched on

The guns of the black-powder wars, for every battery in the book. From the Rules' Modern infantry, only the rule that modern fire puts men down, and only for the breech-loaders: the soldiers' Springfields at the Wagon Box, and the carbines of Fetterman's cavalry and the civilians' repeating rifles. Muskets and rifle-muskets fight as the core rules say. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says, with no antibiotics.

Era Armies A career term Fighting skills

Trouble at work

Thirty Years' War (1618-1648)

d10 Trouble
1 Pay in arrears: no coin this term, only the paymaster's note.
2 The provost asks questions: prove you are not a deserter.
3 Peasants ambush the party: roll a wound.
4 Camp fever or plague: the term is lost to sickness.
5 Taken by the enemy and pressed into their regiment.
6 Robbed by comrades: half the term's take is gone.
7 A wife or comrade is taken by the enemy: ransom or rescue.
8 Debased coin: the pay is worth half.
9 An officer takes the booty as his share.
10 To be hanged as an example, unless someone speaks for him.

Horse and musket (1775-1815)

d10 Trouble
1 A press gang or crimp seizes him: argue or fight.
2 Taken up by the excise or a constable: fine, gaol or transportation.
3 Paid in bad paper or a ticket, worth 60% at best.
4 Fever or flux: the term is lost.
5 Robbed on the road or by a crimp.
6 A mob turns on him: roll a wound.
7 The employer goes bankrupt or flees, owing him.
8 A recruiting sergeant gets him drunk, and he wakes up enlisted.
9 Taken at sea: a prison hulk or Dartmoor.
10 An old crime comes to light: the assizes or a court-martial.

Crimean War (1854-1856)

d10 Trouble
1 Cholera: the term is lost, and a recovery check.
2 Pay stopped: a clerk has lost his name, and he must argue it back.
3 A shell or a stray shot falls on the works.
4 Theft: his kit or his earnings are gone.
5 A drunken brawl with navvies or Zouaves.
6 Accused of selling army stores.
7 Recalled to his regiment at once.
8 Frostbite or exposure on the col.
9 A Cossack patrol near the outposts.
10 An officer wants him as a servant, unpaid.

Civil War and frontier (1861-1876)

d10 Trouble
1 Guerrillas raid the train or the store.
2 The provost guard asks for his papers.
3 Fever or dysentery.
4 The employer skips town owing wages.
5 A stampede or a wagon wreck.
6 Swindled at cards.
7 Mistaken for a deserter.
8 A war party on the trail.
9 A brawl with soldiers.
10 Conscripted on the spot.

Plains nations (1860-1877)

d10 Trouble
1 An enemy war party finds the trail.
2 An army column or patrol.
3 A fall or a goring on the hunt.
4 The trader cheats, or brings whiskey.
5 A blizzard: horses lost.
6 The akicita punish a broken rule.
7 Smallpox or measles in camp.
8 Agency rations are held back.
9 A quarrel over horses or a woman.
10 A rival claims his coup.

What each skill is for

Thirty Years' War (1618-1648)

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Ride Ride hard: Outride a pursuer, or catch a man who rides away. Ordinary the pursuer or the pursued (Ride) Away, or caught. Still close. Thrown: roll a fall as a wound.
Ride Swim a horse: Cross a deep ford or swim a river mounted. Hard — Across. Turned back. Swept away: Endurance check or drowned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Crimean War (1854-1856)

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Ride Ride hard: Outride a pursuer, or catch a man who rides away. Ordinary the pursuer or the pursued (Ride) Away, or caught. Still close. Thrown: roll a fall as a wound.
Ride Swim a horse: Cross a deep ford or swim a river mounted. Hard — Across. Turned back. Swept away: Endurance check or drowned.
Seamanship Handle a boat: Take a boat across a river or along a coast; in rough water, hard. Ordinary — Across. Driven back. Swamped: Endurance check or drowned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.

Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.

Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.

Wound tables

Each battle rolls its wounds on a table built from the record of that war, and these are the notes on where each one comes from. The tables themselves are in the printed tables and the wound roller. A gameplay-adjusted table is re-weighted from bone evidence to stand for every blow that landed, not only the ones that marked bone; an evidence table is the record itself.

Lützen 1632 - mass grave (bone evidence)

Battle injuries on 47 men buried in one grave at Lützen, most likely infantry of the Swedish Blue Brigade cut down by imperial cavalry. Killed only.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Counted from the study's tables of reliable battle injuries (69: 32 projectile, 21 blunt, 16 sharp), each weapon rolling on its own mechanism's injuries. Sides are as recorded; injuries the authors only call probable are left out. Where a bone could belong to more than one location (vertebra, ribcage, cranial base), it is shared by body exposure.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Nicklisch N., Ramsthaler F., Meller H., Friederich S., Alt K.W., 'The face of war: Trauma analysis of a mass grave from the Battle of Lützen (1632)', PLoS ONE 12(5): e0178252 (2017), open access (PMC5439951): Tables 1, 3 and 4.
  • Same study: lead balls in the grave were mostly from carbines (12-14), then muskets (5) and pistols (1-3); 21 men had gunshot wounds to the head; the attack came mainly from the front and side.
  • Injury tally: data/sources/lutzen-1632-mass-grave.csv.

Thirty Years' War - all hits (gameplay)

Where shot and blows land on a man in the open, before death and burial sort the evidence. For pike-and-shot battles of the 1600s.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of the Lützen dead and a stand-in for the wounded; the mix is from casualty totals of a later war.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Lützen 1632; the armies of The Swedish army (Swedes, Finns, Scots and Germans), The Imperial army and the Catholic League.

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 74.5% peninsular-1808-14-officers (wounded) + 25.5% lutzen-1632-mass-grave (killed), location by location.
  • No wounded records survive for the Thirty Years' War; the Peninsular War officers' wounds (same smoothbore lead balls and swords, 180 years later) stand in. Killed share as for the Napoleonic blend (about 1 killed to 3 wounded).

American Revolution 1775-83 - disabled veterans' wounds

Where Continental soldiers, militiamen and seamen were wounded, from the federal invalid pension lists of 1792-95. Men disabled for life who survived.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Counted wound by wound from 344 men's entries (379 wounds whose site is named; 32 more not located). Sides are recorded for about half and were close to even (85 left, 99 right), so left and right are pooled and split by body exposure (design estimate). 'Arm' without more detail is shared between upper arm and forearm.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Federal Revolutionary War Invalid Pension Claims, 1792-1795 (573 veterans), Magazine of Early American Datasets, University of Pennsylvania, 2021; from the Secretary of War's lists printed in American State Papers, Claims, vol. 1.
  • Wound-by-wound tally: data/sources/revolution-invalid-pensions-1792-95.csv. The weapon mix counts the 251 wounds whose cause is stated.

American Revolution 1775-83 - all hits (gameplay)

Where musket balls and shot land on a man in the open, before survival sorts the records.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of a historical wounded table and a stand-in killed table; the mix is from casualty totals.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Cowpens 1781; the armies of The Continental Army (1775-1783), The British Army in America (1775-1783).

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 53.5% revolution-1775-83-pensioners + 46.5% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: Peckham, The Toll of Independence (1974), 7,174 Americans killed and 8,241 wounded in 1,331 land and 218 naval engagements (via Journal of the American Revolution, 'The 25 Deadliest Battles of the Revolutionary War', 2014).

Peninsular War 1808-14 - French officers' wounds

Where French officers were hit in Spain and Portugal, 1808-1814, by musket, sabre, bayonet, lance and cannon. Mostly men who survived.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Location counts are from the source (3,995 wound events). Each weapon rolls on its own recorded distribution (musket 2,848, sword 284, bayonet 97, lance 43, ordnance 209 wounds). Left and right are not recorded and are split evenly; 'arm' (bras) is put on the upper arm because wrist and forearm are listed apart. Rifles and pistols use the musket data.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Planas Campos J. and Grajal de Blas A., 'Wounds & Weapons in the Napoleonic War: a database of the Peninsular War', British Journal for Military History 7(3), Nov 2021, pp. 117-127: Table 1 (weapons, 4,359 entries), Table 2 (locations, 3,995 events), Tables 6-8 (location by firearm, edged weapon and ordnance). Source registers: French Army officer files, SHD 2Yb.
  • Same article, Table 11: 491 rank and file of the 100e de ligne - arms 22%, legs 40%, chest 6%, head 24%, abdomen 1%, shoulder 7% (officers: 26/44/4/14/3/9).
  • Comparison quoted there: Austrian officers wounded at Austerlitz (Guiga 2021) - upper limbs 26%, lower limbs 45%, head 6%, upper body 9%, back 4%.

Napoleonic era - all hits (gameplay)

Where musket balls and shot land on a man in the open, before survival sorts the records. Use for the Peninsula and Waterloo; the War of 1812 has its own table, built from the same records.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of a historical wounded table and a stand-in killed table; the mix is from casualty totals.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Albuera 1811; the armies of The British in the Peninsula (1808-1814), The French Empire in Spain (1808-1814).

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 74.5% peninsular-1808-14-officers + 25.5% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: about one killed for every three wounded in the Anglo-allied army at Waterloo (about 3,500 killed and 10,200 wounded; approximate, commonly cited totals).

War of 1812 - all hits (gameplay, borrowed records)

Where musket balls, rifle balls and shot land on a man in the open or in the woods, before survival sorts the records. No wound count survives for this war; the table is built from the Peninsular War records.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Borrowed: the Peninsular War wounded table blended with a stand-in killed table, at this war's own killed share.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Lundy's Lane 1814; the armies of The United States (1812-1815).

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 66.6% peninsular-1808-14-officers + 33.4% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: US forces lost about 2,260 killed in action and 4,505 wounded (commonly cited totals; British and Canadian losses are usually given only combined).
  • Peninsular War records: Planas Campos and Grajal de Blas, British Journal for Military History 7(3), 2021.

Crimean War 1855-56 - siege of Sevastopol, wounded (surgeons' returns)

British rank and file treated for wounds received in action from 1 April 1855 to the end of the war: almost all of it the siege of Sevastopol (the trenches, the Mamelon, the Redan). Men who reached a surgeon alive.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source: 6,984 gunshot wounds of known region (with 167 sword, bayonet and miscellaneous wounds left out). The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate). The 155 wounds of the larger arteries, nerves and joints of the limbs are shared between arms and legs as the other limb wounds are.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Medical and Surgical History of the British Army which served in Turkey and the Crimea during the war against Russia in the years 1854-55-56 (London, 1858), vol. 2, Part II, Return No. 3 (p. 258) and the returns by region, Section II (pp. 286-339): non-commissioned officers and privates, 1 April 1855 to the end of the war - gunshot wounds of the head 851, face 533, neck 128, chest 420, abdomen (with gunshot fractures of the pelvis) 235, perineum and genito-urinary organs 55, back and spine 326, extremities 4,436 (upper 2,083, lower 2,198, with direct injury of the larger arteries 12 and nerves 22, and penetration of the larger joints 121 by difference); sword, lance and bayonet wounds 41 and miscellaneous wounds 126; 7,161 treated in all.
  • Same work, Return No. 1 (p. 257), for comparison: 14 Sep 1854 - 31 Mar 1855 (the Alma, Balaklava, Inkerman and the first winter's siege), head 206, face 125, neck 64, chest 158, abdomen 100, perineum 15, back and spine 84, extremities 1,763 of 2,515 gunshot wounds of known region (1,815 more unrecorded). Against this period the siege period has 1.5 times the share of head and of face wounds, 1.4 times the back, and fewer limb wounds (63.5% against 70.1%).

Crimean War 1854-56 - all hits (gameplay)

Where Minié bullets, musket balls and shell land on a man in the trenches and works before Sevastopol, before survival sorts the records. Built from the British surgeons' siege returns and a stand-in table for the killed.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of the historical siege wounded table and a stand-in killed table; the mix is from the war's killed and wounded totals.

Rolled by: the battlefields of The Great Redan, 18 June 1855, The Great Redan, 8 September 1855; the armies of British, French, Russian.

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 81.7% crimea-1855-56-siege + 18.3% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: 2,598 British rank and file killed in action in the whole war (Medical and Surgical History of the British Army ... in the Crimea, 1858, vol. 2, Concluding Observations) against 11,595 treated for wounds received in action (Returns Nos. 1 and 3: 4,434 and 7,161).

Civil War 1861-65 - wounded (surgeon's records)

Union soldiers treated for gunshot and shell wounds. Men who reached a surgeon alive.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate).

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Medical and Surgical History of the War of the Rebellion (1870-88), vol. 3, p. 392: head and neck 11%, chest and abdomen 18%, arms and hands 36%, legs and feet 35% of wounds (via Encyclopedia.com, 'Battlefield Wounds').
  • Same work: 35.6% upper extremities, 35.2% lower extremities (via Civil War Monitor, 'Wounded Warriors: Civil War Amputation').

Civil War 1861-65 - killed in action

Seat of the fatal wound in Union soldiers killed in action (n = 1,173).

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate).

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Medical and Surgical History of the War of the Rebellion (1883): seat of injury in 1,173 killed - head and neck 487 (41.6%), trunk 603 (51.4%), upper extremities 30 (2.6%), lower extremities 53 (4.5%) (via US Army, Wound Ballistics in WWII, ch. 6).

Civil War 1861-65 - all hits (gameplay)

Where shots land on a man in the open, before survival sorts the records.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of the two historical tables.

Rolled by: the battlefields of First Bull Run 1861; the armies of The Union (1861-1865), The Confederacy (1861-1865), The US Army on the frontier (1866-1876).

Indian Wars 1865-71 - arrow wounds (US Army surgeons)

Soldiers, scouts and civilians hit by arrows on the Plains and in the Southwest, mostly 1866-70. Killed and wounded together.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Counts are tallied wound by wound from the report's 83 cases (122 arrow wounds whose site is given; 12 more are not located). Left and right are pooled because the sample is small, then split by body exposure (design estimate).

Rolled by: the battlefields of The Fetterman Fight 1866, The Wagon Box Fight 1867; the armies of The Lakota (Oglala, Minneconjou and other bands), The Cheyenne and Arapaho.

Sources:

  • US Surgeon General's Office, Circular No. 3: A Report of Surgical Cases Treated in the Army of the United States from 1865 to 1871 (Washington, 1871), 'Arrow-Wounds', pp. 144-161, cases 451-487. Full text: archive.org item reportofsurgical00unituoft.
  • Same report, p. 161: of 83 cases, 26 'proved fatal', including nearly all that entered the skull, chest or abdomen; 7 of 9 penetrating abdominal wounds were fatal.
  • Wound-by-wound tally: data/sources/indian-wars-arrows-1865-71.csv.

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Lützen, 16 November 1632

  • The armies: Swedes and Imperialists.
  • Fought for: the windmill battery, attacked by the Swedes.
  • The field: 220 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 2,200 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fog, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Thirty Years' War - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Lützen campaign, 1632 (Naumburg to Leipzig), at Lützen.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 541 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

The Swedes crossed the Floßgraben in the early morning and drew up facing the Imperial line behind the high road. Fog delayed the attack until late morning and came and went all day. The Swedish right drove the Imperial left back across the road; in the centre the Swedish foot took the ditches and lost them again. Gustavus Adolphus, riding to help his foot, was killed in the fog. Pappenheim's horse came up on the Imperial left at midday and checked the Swedish right; Pappenheim was mortally wounded. Late in the day Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar's men stormed the windmill hill and its battery, and in the night Wallenstein withdrew. The guns: 7 on the windmill hill and 14 in the Imperial centre, 20 heavy Swedish guns in front of their foot (round figures; the regimental guns are left out).

How the field is drawn

The field of Lützen, 16 November 1632 (Gregorian), at 10 m a hex: 220 x 120 hexes, about 2200 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top. The town, the windmill hill, the road and its ditches and the Floßgraben are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the outline most modern accounts share, in our own words, with round numbers for play.

From exchange Phase What happens

Cowpens, 17 January 1781

  • The armies: Americans and British.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 120 by 100 hexes of 10 m, about 1,200 by 870 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the north-west.
  • Wounds: American Revolution 1775-83 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Cowpens campaign, 1781 (the Pacolet to the Broad), at Hannah's Cowpens.

What happened

Morgan drew up his riflemen in front, the militia behind them, and his Continentals on the crest, with Washington's horse out of sight behind the rise. He asked the riflemen and militia for two volleys each before falling back. Tarleton attacked at once after his night march. The skirmishers and militia fired and fell back round the Continentals' left. When an order to turn the right flank was taken as an order to retreat, the Continentals faced about, halted, turned and fired into the British coming on in disorder, and charged with the bayonet. Washington's horse came in from behind the rise and the militia came back round the other flank; the British line and the 71st were caught between them and surrendered. Tarleton escaped with most of his reserve horse. The morning was cold and clear.

How the field is drawn

The field of Cowpens, 17 January 1781, at 10 m a hex: 120 x 100 hexes, about 1200 m east to west and 870 m north to south, north at the top, the British coming up from the south. The pasture, the two rises, the wet ravines and the woods are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is Morgan's three lines as most modern accounts give them, in our own words, with round numbers for play.

From exchange Phase What happens

Albuera, 16 May 1811

  • The armies: Allies and French.
  • Fought for: the heights south of the allied line, attacked by the French.
  • The field: 150 by 230 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,990 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze.
  • Wounds: Napoleonic era - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Albuera campaign, 1811 (Badajoz to Santa Marta), at La Albuera.

What happened

Godinot's brigade made a show against the village while Girard's and Gazan's divisions, screened by the olive woods, crossed the brooks and came up onto the heights in heavy columns. Zayas's Spaniards turned to face them and held. Colborne's brigade came up on their right and was caught in line by the Polish lancers and hussars in a sudden hailstorm and nearly destroyed. Hoghton's and Abercrombie's brigades took the Spaniards' place and stood exchanging volleys at short range until most of their men were down; Cole's division, coming up on the right, drove the French off the heights. The hailstorm is not set: the GM can bring it in (storm) for the lancers' charge. The guns: 20 French with the columns and 12 allied on the heights (round figures).

How the field is drawn

The field of Albuera, 16 May 1811 (Gregorian), at 10 m a hex: 150 x 230 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 2000 m north to south, north at the top: from the village south over the heights where the battle was decided. The allied line north of the village is off the map. The village, the stream, the woods and the heights are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the moment of Soult's flank attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play.

Lundy's Lane, 25 July 1814

  • The armies: Americans and British.
  • Fought for: the British guns on the crest by the churchyard, attacked by the Americans.
  • The field: 130 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,300 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the south-west.
  • Wounds: War of 1812 - all hits (gameplay, borrowed records).
  • On the travel map: Niagara campaign, 1814 (Fort Erie to Fort George), at Lundy's Lane.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 271 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

Scott's brigade came up the Portage road at about seven in the evening and found Riall's men on the hill with their guns at the churchyard. Scott attacked rather than wait, and his brigade was shot to pieces in front of the guns over the next two hours, though Jesup's 25th worked round the British left in the dusk and took Riall prisoner. Brown brought up Ripley's brigade; in the dark Colonel Miller's 21st Infantry rushed the guns and took them, and the Americans held the crest. Drummond's reinforced line counter-attacked three times until near midnight. Both sides were exhausted; the Americans fell back to Chippawa without the guns. Most of it was fought at night: the phases bring dusk at sunset (about 19:30) and a moonlit night from about 20:00 (a moon about eight days old, more than half lit: sunset and moon are worked out for the place and the day, not from the accounts, which speak of darkness and thick smoke).

How the field is drawn

The field of Lundy's Lane, 25 July 1814, at 10 m a hex: 130 x 110 hexes, about 1300 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top; the Portage road and the Niagara are off the map to the east. The hill, the churchyard, the woods and the fields are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the evening's opening, in our own words, with round numbers for play.

The Great Redan, 18 June 1855

  • The armies: British and Russians.
  • Fought for: the Redan's salient, attacked by the British.
  • The field: 100 by 105 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 910 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Crimean War 1854-56 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Siege of Sevastopol, 1855 (Kamiesh to the Chernaya), at the Great Redan.

What happened

The French and British were to storm the Malakhov and the Redan together after a bombardment, but the Russians had repaired their works in the night and saw the French forming. The French went in early and piecemeal and were thrown back. At daybreak Lord Raglan sent the two flank columns out of the trenches (the centre column, meant to follow, never left them, and is not on the map): riflemen in front, sailors with the ladders, soldiers with wool-bags, then the storming parties. Grape and musketry from the Redan and the batteries either side swept the open ground, and the abatis in front of the work was still whole. The leading men fell within yards of the trenches; Colonel Yea and Sir John Campbell were killed, and the attack was called off. Some 1,400 British were killed, wounded or missing.

How the field is drawn

The first British assault on the Great Redan, Sevastopol, 18 June 1855, at dawn, at 10 m a hex: 100 x 105 hexes, about 1000 m east to west and 910 m north to south, north at the top: the Redan's point toward the British trench at the bottom, about 400 m away, the Karabelnaya suburb behind it. The work and the ground are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map (the point is cut off square, 120 m across, so that units in line can reach it); the deployment is our own reading, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The ladder parties are marked as carrying ladders; on this earthwork (a ditch and a bank, not a wall) the rules give them nothing to do.

The Great Redan, 8 September 1855

  • The armies: British and Russians.
  • Fought for: the Redan's salient, attacked by the British.
  • The field: 100 by 80 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 690 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, strong wind from the north.
  • Wounds: Crimean War 1854-56 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Siege of Sevastopol, 1855 (Kamiesh to the Chernaya), at the Great Redan.

What happened

After three days' bombardment the French stormed the Malakhov, east of the Redan, at noon and held it. On their signal the British went over from the advanced trench, about 200 yards out: a covering party of riflemen, the ladder party, then the stormers of the Light and 2nd Divisions. Many fell crossing the open ground; the ladders were too few and some too short, but men got down into the ditch and up onto the salient. There they stopped and fired from the parapet instead of pressing on, while the Russians fired back from behind their breastwork and traverses and their reserves came up. The supports came forward piecemeal and crowded into the salient. After about an hour and a half a Russian counter-attack drove them back over the parapet and the ditch. That night the Russians blew up their works and left the south side of the town. It was a cold day, with a strong wind and dust.

The work, its ditch, the line either side, the breastwork, the trench, the ravines and the shell holes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map (the point is cut off square, 120 m across, so that units in line can reach it); the deployment is just after noon, in our own words, with round numbers for play. First Bull Run, 21 July 1861

  • The armies: Confederates and Union.
  • Fought for: the top of Henry Hill, attacked by the Union.
  • The field: 140 by 130 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,130 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the south-west.
  • Wounds: Civil War 1861-65 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: First Bull Run campaign, 1861 (Fairfax to Gainesville), at Henry Hill.

What happened

By noon the Union flank march had driven the Confederates off Matthews Hill and over the turnpike. Jackson's Virginians formed on the far edge of Henry Hill with their guns, and the broken brigades rallied behind them. McDowell pushed two regular batteries, Ricketts's and Griffin's, onto the hill near the Henry house with the Fire Zouaves and the Marines in support. The 33rd Virginia, in blue, came out of the woods by the Sudley road and shot down the gunners, and Stuart's horse rode into the Zouaves. The guns changed hands several times through the afternoon. Late in the day fresh Confederate brigades came up on Chinn Ridge to the west, and the Union line broke and streamed back over Bull Run. The day was very hot. Most men on both sides were in their first battle.

How the field is drawn

The hill, the branch, the woods and the ridge are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the early afternoon, in our own words, with round numbers for play.

The Fetterman Fight, 21 December 1866

  • The armies: US Army and Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 150 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Indian Wars 1865-71 - arrow wounds (US Army surgeons).
  • On the travel map: Fort Phil Kearny, 1866 (Red Cloud's War), at Fetterman battlefield.

What happened

The wood train was attacked on its way to the pinery, and Fetterman led a relief out of the fort. Ten decoys, Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho, drew him over Lodge Trail Ridge, against orders, and along its crest. At a signal about a thousand warriors came up out of the ravines and across the flats. The cavalry, ahead, fell back up the ridge; the infantry fought from the rocks; within the hour all 81 soldiers and civilians were dead. The warriors' own losses are put by different accounts at about a dozen to many more. It was the Army's worst loss on the Plains until the Little Bighorn ten years later.

How the field is drawn

The Fetterman Fight, north of Fort Phil Kearny, 21 December 1866, at 10 m a hex: 150 x 120 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the north end of Lodge Trail Ridge down the middle, ravines on both sides, Peno Creek and its flats at the top. The ridge, the ravines, the rocks and the creek are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the moment the decoys turned, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Cold and clear, a little snow on the ground.

The Wagon Box Fight, 2 August 1867

  • The armies: US Army and Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho.
  • Fought for: the wagon-box corral, attacked by the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho.
  • The field: 100 by 80 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 690 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the west.
  • Wounds: Indian Wars 1865-71 - arrow wounds (US Army surgeons).
  • On the travel map: Fort Phil Kearny, 1866 (Red Cloud's War), at Wagon Box corral.

What happened

Warriors struck the woodcutters' camps and ran off the herd, and the men who could reached the corral. Through the morning mounted and foot attacks came at it from several sides; the soldiers' breech-loaders, fired as fast as they could be loaded, held them off. Lieutenant Jenness and two soldiers were killed. In the early afternoon a relief column came out from the fort with a mountain howitzer (it comes on in the last phase; the howitzer itself is not on this map), and the warriors drew off. Estimates of their losses run from a handful to sixty.

How the field is drawn

The Wagon Box Fight, west of Fort Phil Kearny, 2 August 1867, at 10 m a hex: 100 x 80 hexes, about 1000 m east to west and 690 m north to south, north at the top: the plateau between the Big Piney (top) and the Little Piney (bottom), pine woods to the west, a ravine to the east, and the corral of wagon boxes in the middle. The plateau, the creeks, the woods and the ravine are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the corral's exact place was never agreed, and it is drawn as a ring of wagon hexes round two hexes, larger than the real one. The deployment is the first charge, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A hot summer day.
